tagline: A mountain descent follows the Tye past cascades and a gristmill
intro: Crabtree Falls Highway descends from the Blue Ridge Parkway at Tye River Gap into Nelson County’s Tye River valley. The drive follows the South Fork past Crabtree Falls, then the Tye itself, leaving the national forest for gentler terrain just west of Tyro.

The falls became the subject of a preservation effort when plans for a resort emerged in the late 1960s. L.A. Snead, a former U.S. Assistant Fuel Administrator, led negotiations to secure the surrounding land. Personal and congressional funds paid for the land deals, and Snead transferred the deeds to the National Forest System on June 3, 1968.

Traveling east from Tye River Gap, pass through Montebello before reaching Crabtree Falls and Nash. Continue downstream through Tyro, with its historic mill, and Massies Mill toward Roseland. At Roseland, Route 56 turns south to join Route 151 on Patrick Henry Highway.

moments.title: Crabtree Falls
moments.text: Crabtree Falls is a sequence of five major cascades and several smaller ones, fed by Crabtree Creek and draining into the Tye River. The tallest cascade drops about 400 feet. The Forest Service maintains the Crabtree Falls Trail in George Washington National Forest. The land surrounding the falls entered the National Forest System in 1968 after L.A. Snead negotiated purchases in response to resort plans.
moments.notice: The waterfall is a series of cascades, with five major drops and several smaller ones.

moments.title: Tyro
moments.text: Tyro Mill retains the machinery of a nineteenth-century gristmill: wooden gears and drive shafts, two runs of millstones and a husk frame in the basement gear pit. Built in 1846–47, the multistory frame mill received an addition later in the nineteenth century. The building has a metal-clad gabled roof and stone foundation. Outside are an overshot metal wheel in a stone wheel well and remnants of the headrace. The property also includes a mid-nineteenth-century log dwelling, traditionally identified as the miller’s house. The dwelling acquired frame additions and a front porch in the twentieth century.

moments.title: Massies Mill
moments.text: Massies Mill was once the head of the Virginia Blue Ridge Railway, a short line built to carry chestnut lumber from the Piney River area to local mills. After chestnut blight devastated the timber, the railway served quarries producing titanium dioxide and aplite. The railway followed the Tye and Piney Rivers for several miles before entering the mountains. The river valley also suffered catastrophic flooding: on the night of August 19, 1969, the remnants of Hurricane Camille reached Massies Mill. Flash floods and mudslides killed residents here and across the surrounding area. The village then contained forty homes.
